title: Creation, Indexing & Views
blurb: Read grids as coordinates: strided slices, views, and fancy gathers replace every nested loop.

cells.title: A slice is a window, not a copy
cells.body:
When you write g[1:, 1:], numpy does not build a new array. It returns a view: the same memory, described by different strides. That is why slicing a million-row grid costs almost nothing — you are creating a small header object, not copying data.

The consequence cuts both ways. Cheap sub-selection is the foundation of idiomatic numpy, but it also means edits travel: writing into a view silently rewrites the base array. When you hand a slice to unrelated code and want the boundary to be real, reach for .copy(). Keep this in mind throughout this notebook: 'extract a block' exercises are single expressions precisely because views are free.

demo.code:
import numpy as np

g = np.arange(12).reshape(3, 4)
inner = g[1:, 1:]          # a view: same memory, different strides
inner[0, 0] = 99           # writes through to the base grid
print(g)
print(inner.base is not None)  # proof: inner is a view of g

cells.title: Negative and strided slices read like arithmetic
cells.body:
Every slice is three numbers — start, stop, step — and numpy walks them like a range. Negative indices count from the end (-1 is the last row), a negative step walks backwards, and a step of 2 takes every second element along that axis.

The reasoning habit: translate a phrase like 'drop the border' or 'every other row' into one slice per axis. The interior is g[1:-1, 1:-1]; every other row and column is g[::2, ::2]; a left-right mirror is g[:, ::-1]. Composing these lets you express a whole family of rectangular selections with no loops at all — and each slice stays correct when the grid is not square, because nothing is hard-coded.

demo.code:
import numpy as np

g = np.arange(20).reshape(4, 5)
print(g[1:-1, 1:-1])   # interior: drop first/last row and column
print(g[:, ::-1])      # mirror: every row, columns reversed
print(g[::2, ::2])     # every other row and column
print(g[::2, ::2].shape)

cells.title: Fancy indexing gathers (and copies)
cells.body:
A list of indices inside the brackets switches numpy into a different mode: gather. g[[2, 0, 2]] stacks rows 2, 0 and 2 — in that order, repeats allowed — into a new array. With two index lists, g[[0, 2], [1, 3]] pairs them coordinate-wise: elements (0,1) and (2,3).

Unlike slicing, fancy indexing always copies, because the selected elements no longer sit at a constant stride in the source. Gather is the bridge from 'positions I computed' to 'values I want' — you will use it after every argmax, argsort or searchsorted in the later notebooks, so it is worth locking in now.

demo.code:
import numpy as np

g = np.arange(12).reshape(3, 4)
print(g[[2, 0, 2]])        # whole rows, in this order, repeats allowed
print(g[[0, 2], [1, 3]])   # coordinate pairs: elements (0,1) and (2,3)
out = g[[0, 2]]            # fancy indexing copies ...
out[0, 0] = -1
print(g[0, 0])             # ... so the base grid is untouched

exercise.title: Interior Readings
exercise.statement:
A wall of thermal sensors is wired as a grid. The sensors mounted on the frame — the outermost rows and columns — are calibration units and must be excluded from every analysis.

Implement inner_grid(g) so it returns the interior block: all rows except the first and last, and all columns except the first and last. The result must be a 2-D int64 array of shape (R-2, C-2), extracted with a single slice expression — no loops, no np.delete.
constraints: g is a 2-D int64 array with shape (R, C), R >= 3, C >= 3
the result has shape exactly (R-2, C-2) and dtype int64

examples.why: a 3x3 grid has a 1x1 interior: only the center survives
a 3x4 grid keeps rows 1 and columns 1..2, so the interior is 1x2

exercise.starter:
import numpy as np

def inner_grid(g):
    """Return the interior block of grid g (no border rows or columns).

    g is a 2-D int64 array; the result has shape (R-2, C-2).
    """
    pass
hints: The border is exactly one row and one column thick on each side. Which indices does that remove, and how do you say 'everything except index 0 and the last one' in one slice?
Use one slice per axis: rows 1 through R-2 and columns 1 through C-2. In numpy that is g[1:-1, 1:-1] — the negative stop means 'up to but excluding the last'.
Return g[1:-1, 1:-1]. The slice is a view, which is fine here: shape, dtype and values are what get compared, and for R=3, C=3 it correctly yields the single center cell.
exercise.reasoning: A one-thick border removes index 0 and the last index along each axis. The slice 1:-1 says exactly that: start at 1, stop before -1 (which numpy rewrites as the last index), so only rows 1..R-2 survive. Applying it on both axes in one expression keeps the two decisions independent — the row slice never needs to know the column count. That independence is the transferable part: any 'strip the edge' problem (crop an image, drop header and footer rows, remove a margin) becomes one slice per axis, and it stays correct on non-square inputs because nothing is hard-coded. The result being a view also means it is free — no copy of the data is made.
exercise.solution:
import numpy as np

def inner_grid(g):
    """Return the interior block of grid g (no border rows or columns)."""
    return g[1:-1, 1:-1]

exercise.title: Clockwise Perimeter Report
exercise.statement:
The same sensor wall now needs its perimeter reported: a service drone reads the frame sensors while circling the wall clockwise, starting at the top-left corner.

Implement border_ring(g): return a 1-D int64 array of length 2*R + 2*C - 4 holding the border values in clockwise order — top row left to right, right column downward, bottom row right to left, left column upward. Build it from four slices and one concatenate; no loops, no flattening the whole grid.
constraints: g is 2-D int64 with shape (R, C), R >= 2, C >= 2
the output length is exactly 2*R + 2*C - 4 and every border cell appears exactly once
walking order: top row left-to-right, right column top-to-bottom, bottom row right-to-left, left column bottom-to-top

examples.why: top row 0..3, then right column 7, 11, then bottom row backwards 10, 9, 8, then up the left side 4
on a 2x2 the ring is just the four corners in clockwise order

exercise.starter:
import numpy as np

def border_ring(g):
    """Return the border of grid g in clockwise order, starting top-left.

    g is 2-D int64 with shape (R, C), R >= 2, C >= 2. The result is a
    1-D array of length 2*R + 2*C - 4.
    """
    pass
hints: Walk the border by hand on a 3x4 grid and write down the four segments. Which segment must exclude a corner so that no cell is reported twice?

Four slices: the full top row g[0, :]; the right column without its top corner g[1:, -1]; the bottom row without its right corner, reversed g[-1, :-1][::-1]; and the left column without both corners, read upward g[-2:0:-1, 0].
Return np.concatenate([top, right, bottom, left]). Check the piece lengths: C + (R-1) + (C-1) + (R-2) = 2R + 2C - 4, and each corner appears in exactly one segment.
exercise.reasoning: The whole exercise is deciding, for each of the four edges, which corners belong to it. Assign the top-left corner to the top row, the top-right to the right column, the bottom-right to the bottom row, and the bottom-left to the left column — then each edge slice excludes one or both end cells, which is exactly what g[1:, -1], g[-1, :-1][::-1] and g[-2:0:-1, 0] encode. The reversed reads matter because clockwise means the bottom row is consumed right-to-left and the left column bottom-to-top; a negative step flips direction without touching data. Once the four segments are in walking order, one concatenate folds them into the ring, and the length formula 2R + 2C - 4 is a free self-check you can apply to any rectangle.
exercise.solution:
import numpy as np

def border_ring(g):
    """Return the border of grid g in clockwise order, starting top-left."""
    top = g[0, :]                 # full top row, left to right
    right = g[1:, -1]              # right column, without the top corner
    bottom = g[-1, :-1][::-1]      # bottom row, without the last corner, reversed
    left = g[-2:0:-1, 0]           # left column, without both corners, upward
    return np.concatenate([top, right, bottom, left])

exercise.title: Readings at Coordinates
exercise.statement:
A rover on the sensor wall reports a list of (row, column) coordinates it visited — sometimes revisiting the same spot. Given the grid, produce the sequence of readings the rover measured, in visit order.

Implement gather_readings(g, rs, cs): rs and cs are equal-length lists of ints (valid coordinates, repeats allowed). Return a 1-D int64 array whose k-th element is g[rs[k], cs[k]], using one fancy-indexing expression — no loops.
constraints: g is 2-D int64; rs, cs are lists of valid indices with len(rs) == len(cs) >= 1
coordinates may repeat: each occurrence yields its value again
the result is 1-D int64 with length len(rs)

examples.why: the rover stops at (1,0) twice, then (0,1): readings 9, 9, 7

exercise.starter:
import numpy as np

def gather_readings(g, rs, cs):
    """Return the readings at the visited coordinates, in visit order.

    rs[k], cs[k] is the k-th visited cell; coordinates may repeat.
    """
    pass
hints: One index list per axis selects whole rows or whole columns. What does numpy do instead when you put two equal-length index lists in the same brackets?
g[rs, cs] with two lists pairs them elementwise: the k-th output element comes from cell (rs[k], cs[k]). Convert the lists with np.asarray first so numpy definitely sees index arrays.
rs = np.asarray(rs); cs = np.asarray(cs); return g[rs, cs]. Fancy indexing copies, so repeated coordinates simply repeat the value in the output.
exercise.reasoning: Two index arrays in one bracket mean coordinate pairs, not a cross product: numpy zips them, so g[[0, 2], [1, 3]] picks elements (0,1) and (2,3) — exactly the rover's visits, in visit order. This zip semantics is the piece people get wrong: one list gives you rows; two equal-length lists give you one element per pair. Repeats are free, because index arrays describe positions, and the same position may appear many times, each occurrence producing the same value. And since the gathered cells no longer lie at a fixed stride, numpy must copy — which is fine here: the rover wants a reading log, not a view of the wall.
exercise.solution:
import numpy as np

def gather_readings(g, rs, cs):
    """Return the readings at the visited coordinates, in visit order."""
    return g[np.asarray(rs), np.asarray(cs)]

exercise.title: Calibration Checkerboard
exercise.statement:
A camera calibration target is an n×n board where cell (i, j) is painted black (1) when i + j is even and white (0) otherwise.

Implement checkerboard(n): return the n×n int64 board, built without any Python loop and without arithmetic on an index grid — start from np.zeros and paint all black cells with exactly two strided slice assignments.
constraints: cell (i, j) is 1 iff i+j is even; output shape is (n, n), dtype int64
no Python loops: two slice assignments into a zeros array

examples.why: 4x4 board: even rows start with 1, odd rows start with 0
3x3 board: every row is 1, 0, 1 shifted by one

exercise.starter:
import numpy as np

def checkerboard(n):
    """Return the n x n checkerboard with 1 where i+j is even.

    Build it from np.zeros with strided slice assignments; no loops.
    """
    pass
hints: Split the black cells by the parity of the row index: when i is even, what must j be? Which single slice selects exactly those cells in one shot?

i+j is even in exactly two cases: both even or both odd. So paint cells where row and column share a parity: board[::2, ::2] = 1 (even rows, even columns) and board[1::2, 1::2] = 1 (odd rows, odd columns).
board = np.zeros((n, n), dtype=np.int64); board[::2, ::2] = 1; board[1::2, 1::2] = 1; return board. For n=1 the second slice addresses nothing, so the board is [[1]] with no special case.
exercise.reasoning: The parity condition 'i + j even' splits into two lattices: (even i, even j) and (odd i, odd j). Each lattice is exactly what a strided slice selects — ::2 walks every second index starting at 0, 1::2 every second index starting at 1 — so the entire family of black cells is addressed by two slice objects, and numpy paints them at C speed. This is the deepest idea in this notebook: a slice is a pattern, not just a range. Whenever a target set can be described as a lattice — every k-th row, every k-th column, offset starts — a strided assignment builds it in one shot. Edge cases fall out for free: for n=1, board[1::2, 1::2] addresses nothing and the single cell is even-parity, so the result is [[1]] without any special-case code.
exercise.solution:
import numpy as np

def checkerboard(n):
    """Return the n x n checkerboard with 1 where i+j is even."""
    board = np.zeros((n, n), dtype=np.int64)
    board[::2, ::2] = 1     # even rows, even columns
    board[1::2, 1::2] = 1   # odd rows, odd columns
    return board
